name: Somatropin
lead: Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH or HGH), a biosynthetic form of the pituitary hormone whose amino acid sequence matches the natural hormone. It is prescribed to treat growth hormone deficiency in children and adults, and several other conditions involving growth failure or body-composition change, and it has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for these uses since the mid-1980s.[1][2]

Outside those indications, growth hormone is used or discussed for muscle, fat loss, recovery and anti-ageing in bodybuilding and physique communities, where it is often described alongside anabolic steroids and insulin.[16][18] In a 2003 pair of editorials, the New England Journal of Medicine said there was no evidence that HGH is safe and effective in healthy adults or older people, and stressed that the risks of long-term treatment were unknown.[1] Chronic excess of growth hormone occurs in the disease acromegaly, which is described in medical sources by enlargement of bones and soft tissue and is mentioned in forum discussion of facial change.[1][15]

The evidence base is strongest for children with deficiency, where randomized phase 3 trials have compared daily and weekly preparations, and for adults with diagnosed deficiency, where replacement improves body composition and lipids but a long-term mortality benefit has not been shown.[1][4][5]

paras: Growth hormone deficiency is the most common pituitary hormone deficiency and a main cause of short stature in children; a systematic review of nine epidemiological studies found prevalence ranging from about 1 in 1,100 to 1 in 8,600, with heterogeneous populations and diagnostic criteria.[8] Treatment replaces the missing hormone, historically by daily injection. Pediatric indications approved over time include short stature in Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, children born small for gestational age, idiopathic short stature, SHOX deficiency, Noonan syndrome and growth failure in chronic kidney disease.[1][2]

A systematic review of achondroplasia found that growth hormone, vosoritide and limb lengthening all conferred benefits for height or growth velocity, though the long-term effects of growth hormone were unclear.[3]

The Endocrine Society has recommended individualized treatment for adults diagnosed with growth hormone deficiency, with testing in people who have structural pituitary or hypothalamic disease, surgery, irradiation or head trauma, and stringent criteria for the rare diagnosis of idiopathic deficiency in adults.[1][10] Replacement in deficient adults can improve bone density, muscle mass, fat mass and blood lipids, though a long-term mortality benefit has not been demonstrated.[1] US approvals also cover AIDS-associated wasting and short bowel syndrome in adults.[1][2]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: In physique and gear communities, HGH is discussed as an add-on to anabolic steroids and insulin for muscle, leanness and recovery, and some members describe it as a route to faces and physiques that appear 'bigger'; one T Nation commenter attributes a 'phenomenal response' to anabolic steroids and HGH with insulin.[18][15] Members of the same forum describe buying it through gray-market channels, and arguments about whether a particular physique reflects HGH use recur in long threads.[17][15] A 2026 forum post quotes news coverage describing looksmaxxers among those using performance-enhancing drugs, including human growth hormone.[16]

Growth hormone's extra-medical use has been a source of controversy for decades. Wikipedia notes that use of GH as a prescription medicine has been a focus of social and ethical controversy for about fifty years, and that a rhesus-monkey form once featured in the lore of the underground steroid community, with fraudulent versions reportedly sold in gyms.[1]
Most published human trials of somatropin concern children and adults with a recognized medical indication rather than healthy people seeking cosmetic effects.

Pediatric growth hormone deficiency: A 12-month phase 3 trial of 228 prepubertal children compared weekly somatrogon with daily somatropin and found annualized height velocity of 10.10 cm per year versus 9.78 cm per year, meeting the non-inferiority margin.[4] A 52-week phase 3 trial (heiGHt) of 161 treatment-naive children found weekly lonapegsomatropin gave annualized height velocity of 11.2 cm per year versus 10.3 cm per year for daily somatropin.[5] The REAL4 trial of weekly somapacitan in children with deficiency has reported efficacy and tolerability at one year and results at three years.[6][19] A phase 3 trial has also tested somapacitan in children born small for gestational age.[7]

Registered trials: ClinicalTrials.gov lists studies of Genotropin in children with intrauterine growth retardation, Saizen in idiopathic short stature, Omnitrope in short children born small for gestational age, Norditropin in adults with Prader-Willi syndrome, and Serostim in HIV-associated adipose redistribution syndrome.[11][12][13][14]

Metabolism: A randomized trial showed that growth hormone-induced lipolysis and insulin resistance could be abrogated by a ketone body infusion, illustrating the hormone's effects on fat breakdown and glucose handling.[20]

Healthy adults: Wikipedia summarises that there is no evidence that HGH use in healthy adults or older people is safe and effective, and that a small controlled study in critically ill intensive care patients found higher mortality in those given GH.[1] No published trial has tested somatropin for cosmetic facial or body outcomes in healthy people.

Growth hormone treatment usually decreases insulin sensitivity, although some studies of GH-treated adults with hypopituitarism found no increase in diabetes incidence.[1] Earlier concern that GH raised cancer risk was examined in a large study of 6,840 adults treated with GH, which found no overall increase in primary cancer risk over relatively short follow-up, with elevated rates in subgroups defined by age under 35 or childhood-onset deficiency.[1] In August 2011 the FDA issued a safety communication saying evidence on recombinant GH and increased risk of death was inconclusive.[1]

Chronic excess of growth hormone, as in acromegaly, is clinically associated with enlargement of the jaw, brow, hands and feet and with heart and metabolic complications; cadaver-derived growth hormone was linked to Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease before it was withdrawn in 1985.[1][2]

Somatropin binds growth hormone receptors and activates JAK2/STAT signalling, which prompts the liver and other tissues to produce insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and promotes linear bone growth, increases muscle and bone mass, reduces fat mass and influences protein, carbohydrate, lipid and mineral metabolism.[2] It is given by subcutaneous injection, usually once daily; long-acting once-weekly products (lonapegsomatropin, somapacitan, somatrogon) have been tested against daily somatropin in children.[4][5][6]

By the mid-twentieth century endocrinologists understood the features of growth hormone deficiency, but pig and cow hormone did not work in humans because of species differences. In the late 1950s Maurice Raben purified enough GH from human pituitary glands to treat a deficient boy, and in 1960 the US National Pituitary Agency was formed to collect glands and distribute the hormone for research protocols; other countries set up similar agencies. From 1963 to 1985 about 7,700 children in the US and 27,000 worldwide received cadaver-derived GH.[1][9]

In 1981 Genentech, collaborating with Kabi, developed recombinant human GH using recombinant DNA technology. In 1985 four young adults who had received pituitary GH in the 1960s developed Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and use of human pituitary GH rapidly ceased; Genentech's recombinant product, Protropin (methionyl-GH, or somatrem), was approved the same year, with initial treatment costs of US$10,000 to $30,000 per year.[1][2] Subsequent FDA approvals extended indications to chronic kidney disease (1993), adult deficiency (1996), Turner syndrome (1997), Prader-Willi syndrome (2000), small for gestational age (2001), idiopathic short stature (2003), SHOX deficiency (2006) and Noonan syndrome (2007), according to one summary.[2] Lonapegsomatropin was approved in the US in August 2021.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar physique forums, HGH is discussed as a premium addition to steroid regimens, as a presumed cause of particular facial or body appearance, and as an expensive, hard-to-source product.[15][17][18]

claims.claim: HGH use adds to a 'steroid look' and contributes to jaw and facial width
claims.believers: Posters in long T Nation threads argue about whether a physique lacks the 'steroid jawline' only because the person did not use growth hormone, and another thread attributes a 'phenomenal response' to steroids and HGH with insulin.[15][18]
claims.experts: Pubertal facial remodelling is described as involving testosterone together with growth hormone, and chronic GH excess in acromegaly produces bony enlargement; no trial has tested GH as a cosmetic facial treatment in healthy adults.[1]

claims.claim: HGH is a safe anti-ageing and muscle-building therapy for healthy adults
claims.believers: Forum members describe HGH as part of recovery and joint-health routines and discuss obtaining it through informal channels.[17][15]
claims.experts: The New England Journal of Medicine editorials of 2003 stated there is no evidence of safety and efficacy in healthy adults or the elderly; benefits documented in deficient adults include body-composition and lipid changes without proven mortality benefit.[1]

claims.claim: GH combined with insulin and anabolic steroids is an especially effective stack
claims.believers: A T Nation commenter describes a 'phenomenal response' to anabolic steroids and HGH with insulin in the context of discussing physique width.[18]
claims.experts: Published sources describe GH as typically decreasing insulin sensitivity and show lipolysis and insulin resistance as linked effects; no study has tested the combination for appearance.[1][20]

claims.claim: Gray-market HGH is available at stable prices and is genuine
claims.believers: A T Nation member reports ordering HGH and finding prices unchanged.[17]
claims.experts: Wikipedia records that a counterfeit rhesus-GH product circulated in gyms in the steroid underground; GH is a prescription-only drug and prohibited in sport.[1]
